title: How can I prove if this strategy build by my GPT Astra is legit?
author: mojovski
selftext:
I did forward testing, inpexted the charts and use stop loss based on loss, on time and on exposure. Can't think of more risk mitigation methods.

How would you validate this?

comments.author: yeah__good__ok
comments.body: evaluate it the same as any other strategy. If you had it build a strategy without much input then there is almost no chance it will work well though.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Agreed that it gets the same test as any other strategy, and in this case the screenshot is the first thing to fail it, since $400 turning into $313 million points to uncapped position sizing in the test. Where the idea comes from matters less than the evidence: a fixed size, realistic costs and a forward run with frozen rules will show quickly if there's anything there.

replies.author: yeah__good__ok
replies.body: make me a million X strategy. No mistakes.

comments.author: Signal_Pace_7968
comments.body:
The 400 to 313 million is the first thing I’d look at, not as proof but as a warning. That number usually comes from position size growing with the account until the backtest fills orders no real market would fill at that price.

What I’d do, in this order:

1. Rerun it with a fixed size, same lot on every trade. If the edge is real it still shows up as a steady line, just smaller.
2. Put realistic spread and slippage in. Many strategies flip there.
3. Test on a period you never looked at while building it.
4. Compare with random entries using the same exits and size. If random gets close, the exits are doing the work, not the signal.

If it survives all four, a few months on demo is the last step.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: That screenshot is the thing to look at first: turning $400 into $313 million is a sign the test is broken, not a sign of a great strategy. Results like that usually mean position size compounds without a cap (the lot size keeps growing with the balance), the fills ignore spread and slippage, or the data has gaps. To validate it, I'd cap the position at a fixed size so the compounding can't run away, add realistic spread, commission and slippage, and check that the profit isn't coming from a handful of giant trades. Then run it forward on a demo account for a few weeks with the rules frozen and compare those live fills with what the test assumed. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to see how strategy results get compared against a benchmark.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: stops cap the damage, they don't prove an edge. what does: 100+ trades, the same rules on a stretch the GPT never saw, and the result next to random entries with the same stops. I built Quantradin after doing that by hand one time too many: describe the rule, it gets tested on real past prices, then runs on fake money, free. quantradin.com. how many trades does your forward test have?

comments.author: _PolyWasp_
comments.body: It's pretty easy to validate this. You see the initial deposit and the net profit and you know right away it's not valid.

comments.author: Other-Hurry9870
comments.body:
Paper trade it on a platform that supports prompts. Costs $0 and literally takes 1 minute.

Run it with AI. Come back in 2 weeks and check if it made money.

comments.body: Proof is already there that strategy doesn't work. 400 to 300 million lol. GPT just did a serious overfit for your tests

comments.author: VindictiveHydrogen24
comments.body: I believe  this is what they call fine tuning. The strategy will most likely fail in the real world. But test it regardless
